newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Confident Spain may outperform new plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Confident Spain may outperform new plan.

text.p: Spain on Tuesday brushed aside criticism that a new three-year fiscal discipline plan designed to bolster its bid to join Europe's single currency was over-ambitious, saying it might outperform the targets.

"(Last year) no one in the markets believed we could reach our objectives on inflation and long-term interest rates. We beat the markets (then) and we haven't finished beating them," Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro told journalists.

Details of the new plan, which pledges fiscal discipline into the next century, were released this week. Set for cabinet approval on Friday, the plan foresees public debt falling to 65.3 percent of gross domestic product in 2000 from 68.2 percent in 1997.
This fulfils the European economic and monetary union (EMU) requirement of achieving a decline in debt levels but falls short of the 60 percent reference value set by the Maastricht Treaty.

The deficit is seen declining to 1.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from a projected 3.0 percent this year and 4.4 percent in 1996. This would be far below the 3.0 percent prerequisite for joining the launch of the euro.
Average growth is seen at 3.2 percent through the year 2000.
"I emphasise that this is relatively gentle (growth and) we could manage a deficit reduction to under 1.6 percent. We could do better," Montoro said. "But we have to be realistic."
To ensure it meets the new objectives, the government will pursue austere budgets and market liberalisation.
"We are applying the measures that we know how to apply. We are applying the measures we had planned to use," he said.
Confident of the plan and bolstered by widespread support at home for its bid to join the single currency, the government will submit it to parliamentary debate -- the only European country to do so.
"We want to go to Brussels with the backing of the entire country," Montoro said.

In the scant year since the conservatives took the helm after 13 years of Socialist rule, inflation and long-term interest rates have declined sharply, while the peseta has stabilised -- fulfilling three of the Maastricht criteria.
The government has also pledged to adhere to criteria stipulating lower deficit and debt levels.
While convinced it will make the cut next spring for EMU based on 1997 data, Spain is acutely conscious that its short history of economic stability causes great unease among its European brethren.

Early this year, German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark said some countries did not have the track record to join the euro launch. Although he named no names, market participants believed he was targeting Italy, Spain and Portugal.
"With the passport we carry, it isn't possible for anyone to say 'no'," Montoro said. "It isn't that we don't have a present. It's that we don't have a past and we want to have a future."
